\title{Every Added Test Raises the Mutation Score:\\
A Pitfall in Evaluating Mutation Testing on Bug Fixes, and a Kill-Matrix Protocol}

\ifanonymous
\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Anonymous Author(s)}}
\else
\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Kanhaiya Mehta}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Independent researcher\\
kanhaiyakumar76618@gmail.com}}
\fi

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Bug-fix commits are an attractive source of real faults for evaluating mutation testing: the tests a fix
adds catch the bug, so one can compare the mutation score (MS) of the suite without them ($\Tbase$) and
with them ($\Taug$). We show that this comparison is uninformative by construction: $\Taug$ contains
$\Tbase$, so its MS can never be lower, whatever the added tests do. On \PitfallPairs{} bug fixes in
Apache Commons Lang, the naive comparison finds a gain in all \NaivePositivePairs{} pairs (sign test
$p=\NaiveSignP$), yet removing the same number of random tests that reveal no bug makes the same test
``significant'' in \PlaceboSigShare{} of \PlaceboDraws{} placebo replicates. We propose a protocol that
avoids the pitfall: measure which tests reveal the bug, record PIT's full kill matrix, check comparisons
against a placebo, and compare test subsets of equal size. At equal size, MS ranks bug-revealing subsets
above the others with a median $\hat{A}_{12}$ of only \RqOneMedianMS{}, no better than coverage
(\RqOneMedianCov{}), and the arithmetic and boundary operators that the naive analysis singled out carry
no signal (\SelectionMedian{}). The pilot is small; its contribution is the pitfall, the placebo check, and
an auditable protocol whose scripts generate every number in this paper.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
mutation testing, test adequacy, real faults, empirical methodology, replication
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
Mutation testing measures how adequate a test suite is by the share of injected faults (mutants) that its
tests detect~\cite{coles2016pit}. Whether a higher mutation score means better detection of real faults has
been studied with real-fault benchmarks~\cite{just2014mutants,just2014defects4j} and remains debated: much of
the reported correlation comes from test-suite size~\cite{papadakis2018mutation,inozemtseva2014coverage}, and
asking for a correlation at a fixed size may itself be the wrong question~\cite{chen2020revisiting}. The
question is again pressing as tests are generated by LLMs~\cite{zhao2026coverage} and guided by targeted
mutants in industry~\cite{foster2025mutation}.

Bug-fix commits look like an ideal laboratory: the developer adds a test that fails before the fix and
passes after it. A natural design compares the mutation score of the suite without the added tests
($\Tbase$) with that of the post-fix suite ($\Taug$) and asks whether the gain is positive across many
fixes. Our first analysis of the pilot data reported here took exactly this route and obtained a highly
significant result. This paper explains why such a result is meaningless and what to do instead:
\begin{itemize}
\item the \emph{monotonicity pitfall} of base-vs-augmented comparisons, and a placebo check that exposes it
on real data (Sec.~\ref{sec:pitfall});
\item a \emph{kill-matrix protocol} that measures fault-revealing tests directly and compares equal-size test
subsets without re-running the mutation tool (Sec.~\ref{sec:protocol});
\item a pilot on \PitfallPairs{} Commons Lang fixes, with all data and scripts released
(Sec.~\ref{sec:pilot}).
\end{itemize}

\section{The Pitfall}\label{sec:pitfall}
Let $M$ be the mutants of the fixed program and $K(m)$ the tests that kill mutant $m$. For a test suite $S$,
$\MS(S) = |\{m \in M : K(m) \cap S \neq \emptyset\}|\,/\,|M|$. If $S \subseteq S'$, every mutant killed by $S$
is killed by $S'$, so $\MS(S) \le \MS(S')$. Since $\Taug = \Tbase \cup A$ for the added tests $A$,
\begin{equation}
\Delta\MS = \MS(\Taug) - \MS(\Tbase) \ge 0 \quad \text{for every } A,
\end{equation}
and $\Delta\MS > 0$ as soon as $A$ kills one mutant that $\Tbase$ misses, which holds for almost any new
test, whether it reveals the bug or not. A sign test across $n$ fixes then only counts non-zero gains: if all
are positive, its two-sided $p$-value is $2^{1-n}$, below $0.05$ for every $n \ge 6$. The comparison is also
confounded with size, since $\Taug$ is always the larger suite~\cite{papadakis2018mutation}. Only
nondeterminism, such as timeouts that differ between two mutation runs, can make $\Delta\MS$ negative, and
that is noise rather than signal.

The pitfall is easy to fall into because every step looks reasonable: the added tests do reveal the bug,
they do raise the score, and the test is significant. What is missing is a comparison that could have come
out the other way. Section~\ref{sec:protocol} adds two: a placebo and equal-size subsets.

\section{Protocol}\label{sec:protocol}
\subsection{Pairs and fault-revealing tests}
We mine single-parent commits whose message mentions a fix and that change production code and add test
methods (methods present after the fix but not before). The post-fix test classes are applied to the buggy
version $V_{\mathit{bug}}$ and run with Surefire; the test methods that fail are the fault-revealing tests $F$.
A compile error is not a detection: such pairs are skipped and logged. $\Tbase$ is the post-fix test class
with the added methods disabled (only their own JUnit annotations are commented out). We require $\Tbase$ to
be green on the fixed version without the added tests, and $\Taug$ to be green with them.

\subsection{Kill matrix}
We run PIT~\cite{coles2016pit} on the fixed version with the full mutation matrix enabled, so each mutant
lists every test that kills it and every test that runs it without killing it. From the matrix we compute,
for any subset $S$ of $\Taug$, the mutation score $\MS(S)$ and a coverage score $\COV(S)$: the share of mutants
executed by at least one test in $S$. Mutants that PIT counts as detected without naming a test (timeouts and
memory errors, at most \LeftOutMax{} per pair here) cannot be attributed and are left out. As a check, the
matrix reproduces PIT's own killed count for $\Taug$ exactly in \MatrixExactPairs{} of \RqOnePairs{} pairs,
and the count for $\Tbase$, measured in a separate run, within \MatrixMaxBaseDiff{} mutant.

\subsection{Placebo}\label{sec:placebo}
For each pair we remove $|A|$ random tests that do not reveal the bug from $\Taug$, \PlaceboDraws{} times, and
compute the same $\Delta\MS$. Per pair, $p_{\mathrm{pl}}$ is the share of placebo draws whose gain is at
least the real one. Across pairs, we apply the naive sign test to every placebo replicate (one draw per pair).

\subsection{Equal-size subsets}\label{sec:subsets}
For sizes of \SubsetSizes{} of the suite, we draw \SubsetDraws{} random subsets of exactly $k$ tests; a subset
detects the bug if it contains a test in $F$. At each size we compute Vargha and Delaney's
$\hat{A}_{12}$~\cite{vargha2000critique}: the chance that a random detecting subset scores higher than a random
non-detecting one, where $0.5$ means the score says nothing beyond size. Sizes with fewer than
\MinGroupSubsets{} subsets in either group are skipped. Per pair we report the median over sizes, and we test
across pairs with two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. For operators, subsets are scored on the mutants of one
operator, in pairs where it has at least \MinKillable{} mutants killed by some test.

\subsection{Auditability}
The analysis scripts write every number, table and figure of this paper from the raw PIT and Surefire reports
(the paper only includes the generated files), so no result is typed in by hand.

\section{Pilot Study}\label{sec:pilot}
We apply the protocol to Apache Commons Lang with PIT 1.16 (\texttt{STRONGER} mutators), JUnit~5 and JDK~21;
the test pool of a pair is its changed test classes. Of \CandidatesMined{} mined candidates,
\CandidatesSkipped{} add no test method and are skipped, leaving \PitfallPairs{} pairs with \TotalTests{} test
methods, \TotalAdded{} added tests and \TotalFaultRevealing{} fault-revealing ones (Table~\ref{tab:pairs}).

\textbf{RQ1: Does the base-vs-augmented comparison tell bug-revealing tests apart?} The naive comparison finds a
gain in all \NaivePositivePairs{} pairs (sign test $p=\NaiveSignP$). The placebo makes the same test
significant in \PlaceboSigShare{} of the replicates (median $p=\PlaceboMedianPValue$), although the removed tests
reveal no bug. Only in \RealBeatsPlaceboPairs{} pairs do the added tests raise the score more than 95\% of the
placebo removals (Fig.~\ref{fig:placebo}): a random existing test often kills as many unique mutants as the
bug-revealing one.

\textbf{RQ2: At equal size, does MS rank bug-detecting suites higher?} Mutation score ranks detecting subsets
higher in \RqOneMSAbove{} of \RqOnePairs{} pairs, with a median $\hat{A}_{12}$ of \RqOneMedianMS{}
($p=\RqOnePms$ against $0.5$). Coverage does about as well: median \RqOneMedianCov{}, above $0.5$ in
\RqOneCovAbove{} pairs ($p=\RqOnePcov$). Mutation score beats coverage in \RqOneMSBeatsCov{} pairs, and the
difference is not significant ($p=\RqOnePdiff$). In Table~\ref{tab:pairs}, the two highest values (Instants and
CharRange) belong to pairs whose added tests kill many mutants that no other test kills (their large
$\Delta$MS); for Conversion, coverage separates the subsets even better than mutation score.

\textbf{RQ3: Which operators carry the signal?} Table~\ref{tab:ops} scores each operator separately. The
MATH + boundary selection that the naive analysis singled out has a median $\hat{A}_{12}$ of \SelectionMedian{}
(above $0.5$ in \SelectionAbove{} of \SelectionPairs{} pairs) while covering \SelectionShare{} of all mutants.
The best single operator, \texttt{\BestOperator}, reaches \BestOperatorMedian{} (above $0.5$ in
\BestOperatorAbove{} of \BestOperatorPairs{} pairs), a small effect.

\section{Discussion and Threats to Validity}
\textbf{Recommendations.} (1) Do not present $\MS(\Taug) - \MS(\Tbase)$ as evidence that mutation score tracks
bug detection. (2) Report a placebo, or compare equal-size suites. (3) Decide fault detection per test method
from test reports, not from the build outcome, which also fails on compile errors. (4) Release kill matrices,
so that others can re-analyze without re-running the mutation tool.

\textbf{Threats.} The pilot has \PitfallPairs{} pairs from one project. Per-pair $\hat{A}_{12}$ values describe
random subsets of one test class, not a population of real suites. Operator results rest on few mutants per
pair. Mutants detected only by timeout are excluded. The placebo removes existing tests rather than adding new
tests that reveal no bug. These threats limit how far the pilot results generalize, but not the pitfall, which
follows from set inclusion alone.

\section{Future Plans}
We will (i) scale up with candidates already mined from Apache Commons CSV and Gson and with
Defects4J~\cite{just2014defects4j,laurent2022revisiting}, pre-registering the analyses; (ii) study the
probabilistic question raised by Chen et al.~\cite{chen2020revisiting}: does adding a test that kills more
mutants make detecting a fault more likely than adding a random test; (iii) compare selective mutation with
random mutant sampling at an equal budget~\cite{gopinath2016limits}, with execution times measured without the
full matrix; (iv) revisit fault revelation without assuming a clean program~\cite{chekam2017empirical}; and
(v) apply the placebo to evaluations that add generated tests to a suite, such as LLM-generated or
mutation-guided tests~\cite{foster2025mutation,zhao2026coverage}, where the same pitfall applies.
